stops.text: Start at the boundary. The plasma membrane encloses roughly 5,000 µm³ of a hepatocyte and carries the pumps and receptors that link the cell to the blood.
The nucleus holds the genome and occupies about 6% of the cell volume. Its envelope is a double membrane that is continuous with the endoplasmic reticulum.
Thousands of nuclear pore complexes perforate the envelope. Each is built from about 30 different nucleoporins and gates traffic between nucleus and cytoplasm.
Inside the nucleus, nucleoli assemble ribosomal subunits from rRNA and ribosomal proteins.
Ribosome-studded ER sheets wrap the nucleus. Here hepatocytes make secreted plasma proteins such as albumin.
Proteins move on to the Golgi apparatus, a ribbon of stacked cisternae next to the centrosome, where they are modified and sorted.
The centrosome, with its two orthogonal centrioles, is the main organizer of microtubules.
Microtubules radiate from the centrosome and act as tracks for motor proteins that move organelles and vesicles.
Mitochondria fill 22% of a hepatocyte's volume, about 1,700 of them. They produce ATP and run fatty-acid oxidation and the first steps of the urea cycle.
Peroxisomes oxidize very-long-chain fatty acids and break down hydrogen peroxide with catalase.
Endosomes sort material taken up from the cell surface: receptors are recycled, cargo is sent onward for degradation.
Lysosomes are acidic compartments with about 40 kinds of hydrolytic enzymes that break down macromolecules.
Ribosomes translate mRNA into protein, free in the cytosol or bound to the rough ER. A real cell has millions; only a sample is drawn.
Keratin 8/18 intermediate filaments give hepatocytes mechanical resilience and protect them against stress.
